intro: Fifteen programs (n-body, fannkuch-redux, spectral-norm, binary-trees, mandelbrot, fasta and k-nucleotide in the style of the Computer Language Benchmarks Game; sieve of Eratosthenes, string manipulation, heap graph search, sorting and searching, LRU cache, Merkle tree, JSON serialise and parse, and hello world written for this suite) in {nlang} languages, single-threaded, on a 2-core Linux VM. The page is grouped by metric (execution time, compile time, peak memory, executable size) and then by program; each metric opens with one table of every language on every program, and its column headers sort it.
footer: Time is the fastest run; memory is the median peak resident size (wait4 on a small launcher); compile time is the median of the builds, wall clock. Output of every implementation is compared with the C -O0 build at the same size. “Everything on” = every optimizer pass at its most aggressive setting plus register variables and temporaries; “off” = every optimisation switch off.
notes: **Memory-safe views.** Every bar chart and every overview table is repeated with only (a) Caspien’s safe variants (naive, optimized safe, struct nodes safe, and the programs that have no unsafe-dynarray variant at all; every Caspien program still uses `unsafe` blocks for libc calls and, in a few, globals) and (b) implementations whose runtime or compiler provides memory safety: Java, Kotlin (JVM), C# (.NET, built without AllowUnsafeBlocks), Go, Node and Bun (JavaScript engines), LuaJIT, OCaml, Swift, Crystal, and Rust — Rust only for programs that rustc accepts under `-F unsafe_code` (tools/rust_safe_check.py; only the heap-graph port fails). That is a property of the implementation, not a judgement of the sources. Caveat, not a filter: some ports use their language’s unchecked escape hatches (LuaJIT `ffi` buffers, OCaml `unsafe_get`, Swift `UnsafeMutablePointer`), which a runtime-level guarantee does not cover. Excluded as languages: C, C++, Objective-C, Fortran, Odin, Zig, Chapel, D, Nim, Codon and WebAssembly.

**Toolchains added on 1 Oct 2026.** Fortran (gfortran), Objective-C (gcc + GNU libobjc, no Foundation), D (LDC and GDC), Nim 1.6 (refc), Crystal, OCaml (no flambda), Swift 6.0.3 (-O, static stdlib, Glibc only), Codon 0.17, Zig 0.16 (ReleaseFast: no safety checks), Odin (-o:speed, bounds checks on), Chapel 2.3 (--fast), C# (.NET 8, tiered JIT, PGO), Kotlin 2.0.21 (JVM), WebAssembly (the C program built with zig cc for wasm32-wasi, ahead-of-time compiled by wasmtime 25). All of them single-threaded, compiled with the normal release flags; every port reproduces the C program's output exactly (checked at every size that was run).
**Dart is missing.** Its toolchain could not be downloaded: the sandbox network allowlist blocks the Dart SDK hosts. Nothing was substituted.

**Ports are idiomatic, not identical.** Each port does the same work with the same algorithm and the same data-structure kind as the C, Rust, Go or Java program it follows, but uses its own language's containers where those exist (Dictionary, HashMap, associative arrays, Table); garbage-collected and reference-counted languages allocate nodes the way a programmer in that language would. Differences worth knowing are noted in the port files and in docs/RESULTS.md.

**Size.** Java, C# and Kotlin count the runtime (JRE or the .NET shared runtime) plus the program; Node and Bun the interpreter binary plus the script; WebAssembly the wasmtime binary plus the .wasm; native binaries only themselves. Zig and Swift link a static runtime. This makes the size column about _deployment size_, not code size.

**Compile time** is wall clock of the whole build (Caspien: its four stages plus assembler and linker; Zig: a cold cache build; C#: dotnet build; WebAssembly: zig cc plus wasmtime compile). Node, Bun and LuaJIT have no compile step.
**Memory** is the peak resident size of the process (wait4). Garbage-collected runtimes size their heaps from the machine, so their peaks reflect policy as well as need.

**Heap graph, binary trees, LRU:** Caspien structs can only point at themselves through a plain nullable `ref`; the default rows are index-based, the _ref_ rows use real linked nodes (every deref under a ghost-table alive proof, so they are much slower); the other languages use pointers or references. Same work, not the same memory layout. _ref in stdlib_ = the same naive program with the stdlib HashMap replaced by a separate-chaining version built on `ref` nodes (`stdlib/ref/hash_map.caspien`).

**Sorting:** Caspien elements are u64, the others use 32-bit integers. **Linux only:** nothing was run on the Windows targets. **Noise:** a 2-core VM, timings vary by roughly 5–10% between runs; time is the fastest run.

**Re-run on 4 Oct 2026** after the allocation-free insecure_hashOf, leaner HashMap, constant-division, sqrt and loop-unrolling changes: every program, every language, fastest of 3 runs, compile time the median of 2 builds, Linux 2-core VM, every output equal to the C reference.

**Quick and full runs.** A _full_ run builds every Caspien variant with optimisations off and on, repeats everything 5 times (compile time: median of 3 builds) and runs every language to completion. A _quick_ run builds only the optimised Caspien variants, measures them first, and kills any other implementation whose first run reaches the slowest optimised Caspien time of that program (at least 0.1 s). Such a row is a full-colour bar at that limit, labelled “> limit (cut off)”, meaning _would have taken longer than optimized Caspien_; it has no peak-memory figure, its ratios and the geometric mean are lower bounds (≥), and it has no output to compare. Quick files carry `mode` and `cutoff_s`.

**Gold lines** (execution-time charts only; the other metrics are measured once per build): two lines at the best time minus and plus the typical run-to-run noise, defined as the median of the three repeats minus the best one. A single stray slow repeat (a JIT pause, a noisy neighbour) does not stretch them; the hover text also gives the slowest repeat. The value text sits to the right of the rightmost line.

**Colours**: green = Caspien (hatched = optimisations off / naive, solid = everything on), red = bare metal and natively compiled languages, purple = compiled and interpreted (JVM, .NET, WebAssembly), blue = interpreted (Node, Bun, LuaJIT); shades tell the languages apart; every row is also labelled with its language, so colour is never the only cue (a palette of 24 languages cannot be colour-blind-safe by colour alone).

recursion.intro: what does the recursion-to-loop conversion cost, and could real recursion ever win?

chain.title: Chain: tail recursion against a loop
chain.note: Linear tail recursion, depth {depth} repeated {reps} times. A true loop is the baseline: a recursive form only ever ties it (when the compiler or runtime turns the tail call into a jump) or loses to it.

tree.title: Tree: non-tail recursion against an explicit stack
tree.note: Visit every node of a complete binary tree of depth {tree} (non-tail recursion). Here the native call stack beats an explicit stack; the Rust row is constant-folded by LLVM and means nothing.

bullets: **Result.** Recursion never beat a loop. gcc, g++ and rustc -O2 turn the tail call into the same loop (tie); Go and Java do not eliminate tail calls (about 5× slower); LuaJIT has proper tail calls (tie). For non-tail recursion the native stack beats a hand-written explicit stack (about 4× at C -O2).
**Caspien.** `@recursive` is lowered to a bounded `for` by the compiler, so there is no call stack; the lowered loop still costs about 2.5× a hand-written loop (range rebuilt and tested per step).
**Caveats.** Node and Bun chain times (6–15 s, even for the hand loop) are probably 64-bit BigInt emulation, not recursion cost. The Rust tree row is constant-folded.
